pick.kicker: Recommendation for Kaabil · offline on a 2 GB Android phone
pick.title: Ship Piper as the offline floor, Supertonic 3 as the quality tier, and pre-render the fixed prompts
pick.body: No single small model wins on all three of your constraints (Hindi + Marathi, tiny, fast on a weak CPU), so split the job.
points: Fixed prompts (most of a form flow): don't synthesise them on the phone at all. Field labels, consent questions and warnings are a finite list. Render them once with the best voice you can get (a commercial Indic voice, or Kokoro for Hindi), ship them as small audio files, and keep live TTS for the dynamic parts: names, numbers, job details.

Offline floor: Piper through sherpa-onnx. 64–77 MB per language, about 210 MB of RAM, 25x faster than real time on this laptop, and the only tiny model here with a real Marathi voice. It is the least expressive and its Marathi is rough, but it is the only one that will certainly keep up on a 2 GB phone.

Quality tier for better phones and for Hindi/English: Supertonic 3 (int8, 145 MB). One model for every language, 44.1 kHz audio, Hindi as intelligible to Whisper as the Microsoft cloud voice, reads Hinglish as written, and needs no espeak-ng. Never feed it raw digits.

Kokoro-82M is the best small voice for English and Hindi on a laptop or server (lowest error of the local models), but at about 2x real time on a laptop CPU it will fall behind real time on a low-end phone, and it has no Marathi.

Online path (WhatsApp bot, IVR callback): use a server voice. Sarvam Bulbul or BHASHINI / AI4Bharat for Hindi and Marathi. That is where the truly human-sounding voices are; none of them fit on the phone.

Whatever you pick, put a text front-end before it. Every local model failed on raw numbers, and two silently skipped digits or English words. Scenarios 3 vs 4 and 5 vs 6 let you hear what the front-end buys.

caveat: How these numbers were made: I cannot listen to audio. Every clip was transcribed by Whisper large-v3-turbo and compared with the script ('ASR error'), and pitch, pauses, bandwidth and speed were measured from the signal. That captures intelligibility and pacing, not whether a voice sounds warm, human or correctly accented. Whisper is itself imperfect in Marathi: the Microsoft cloud voice scores 14% error there, so treat that as the floor, not as zero. The naturalness verdict has to come from Hindi and Marathi listeners using the blind test on the Listen tab. Speed was measured on a laptop that heats up under load; repeat runs differed by up to 2x. Nothing was measured on a phone.
method: Mean ASR error is over the seven single-speaker scenarios that are scored (form guidance, hurry, scam warning, consent, slow repeat, long read, tongue twister). Numbers and mixed-script scenarios are judged from the transcript instead, because Whisper spells digits and English words its own way.

piper.verdict: The safe offline floor. Tiny, very fast, real Hindi and Marathi voices; the flattest delivery and the weakest Marathi.
good: 25x faster than real time on 4 CPU threads (median); a 30-second paragraph took about 1 second.
63–77 MB per voice and about 210 MB RAM with one voice loaded: the smallest footprint with Indian languages.
The only tiny model here trained on Marathi. Runs on Android through sherpa-onnx.
English ASR error 1.0%, as clear as models five times its size.
You can fine-tune it on your own recordings, which no other model here allows as easily.
bad: Hindi ASR error 9.7% against 5–6% for Kokoro and Supertonic. The polite imperative बताइए was heard as बताई दे / बताईगे in two different scenarios.
Marathi ASR error 24.7%, nearly double the cloud reference (14%). The stock voice comes from a small crowd-sourced multi-speaker set.
English voice has the least pitch movement of any engine (±1.8–2.3 semitones against 3–4.5): the scam warning sounds like the form prompt.
Raw numbers: phone number read as 'ninety-eight thousand…', the date as a string of digits, and 5:30 came out as '35, 30' in Hindi.
English words inside Hindi text are mangled (mobile number verify heard as मोबाल नम्ब बैफ़ाइ).

Barely pauses: 0.6 s of silence in the Hindi form prompt where the cloud voice leaves 3.2 s, so phrases run together. The speed control also under-delivers (a 1.4x request gave 1.29x, 0.75x gave about 0.8x).
fix: Normalise text first: expand numbers, dates and ₹, read OTPs digit by digit, write English words in Devanagari. Scenario 6 shows Piper becoming clearly intelligible on the same Hinglish sentence.
Add the missing pauses yourself: synthesise phrase by phrase and insert 300–600 ms of silence. This matters more for elderly listeners than the speed setting.
Raise noise_scale / noise_w a little for a livelier read, and compare by ear.
Fine-tune the Marathi voice on a single-speaker studio set (IndicTTS, SYSPIN or your own 1–2 hours). This is the highest-value model work for Kaabil.

kokoro.verdict: Best small voice for English and Hindi on a laptop or server. No Marathi, and too slow for a 2 GB phone.
good: Lowest ASR error of the local models: English 0.7%, Hindi 5.0% (the cloud reference scored 7.1% on the same sentences, so this is at Whisper's noise floor).
Follows the speed control closely: a 1.4x request gave 1.47x and 0.75x gave 0.73x.
4 Hindi and 28 English voices, enough distinct speakers for the three-way conversation test.
Apache-2.0 weights; the 8-bit build is 121 MB including the voice pack.
bad: About 2x real time on this CPU. A low-end phone is several times slower, so expect it to fall behind real time there. The 8-bit build was not faster on this laptop.
Pitch movement is nearly identical in every scenario (±2.8–3.0 semitones for calm, urgent and slow alike). There is no emotion or style control.
Slows down by stretching the sounds (speech 34% longer at 0.75x), which gets droney; it does not add thinking pauses.

The stock kokoro-onnx package has two Hindi bugs: it speaks espeak's language markers aloud ('आपका in application hi submit…') and drops the danda, so sentences run together. Both are patched in rig/engines.py; the clips here use the patch.
Raw Hindi numbers: the phone number was read as a quantity (अट्ठानवे हज़ार सात सौ पैंसठ…) and 'DigiLocker' became दिगी लौका.
Marathi only works by reading it through a Hindi voice: 13.6% ASR error, the ळ sound is lost (कळवा heard as कवा), and overlapped Marathi speech fell apart (45.8%).
fix: Keep the phonemiser patch (language_switch='remove-flags', danda to full stop) and report it upstream.
Synthesise and play sentence by sentence so the listener waits for one sentence, not the whole reply.
With no style control, create urgency in the text: shorter sentences, exclamation marks, speed 1.15–1.25.
Use it as the offline renderer for your fixed Hindi and English prompts rather than as the on-phone engine.

supertonic.verdict: Best balance for a phone-sized multilingual model: clean audio, reads Hinglish as written. Must never be given raw digits.
good: Hindi ASR error 5.9%, level with the cloud reference; about 3.6x real time at 8 steps in the batch run.
Latin-script English inside Hindi and Marathi sentences came through intact with no transliteration step. No other local model managed that.
Crispest audio: 14–22 kHz of real bandwidth at 44.1 kHz (Piper 11 kHz, MMS 8 kHz).
Exact speed control (1.4x request gave 1.40x) and it slows down the way people do: at 0.75x pauses doubled while the words got only 13% longer.
Held up best when speakers overlap: 1.1% error on the Hindi crosstalk mix, where Piper and Kokoro lost 13–14%.
No phonemiser, so no espeak-ng (GPL) in your app; one 145 MB int8 model covers every language; 10 voices.
bad: Raw digits are dangerous. In Hindi the OTP '4 8 2 9 1 6' was heard as '5829200' and the wage and date became unrelated syllables; in English a phone digit vanished and ₹ was read as a dollar amount.
Even with digits spelled out, Whisper heard five of the six Hindi OTP digits, and 'Quick, quick' lost one 'quick'. Flow-matching models occasionally skip a token.
Marathi is not a supported language. Feeding Marathi text with the Hindi tag scored 10.9% ASR error, better than the native Piper voice, but the accent is unverified and ळ is dropped.
Cutting synthesis steps to save time costs Hindi clarity quickly: 3.6% error at 8 steps, 5.6% at 5, 8.6% at 4, 15.8% at 3. English tolerated 3 steps.
At 0.75x on the numbered list, 43% of the clip is silence (8.4 s of 19.5 s). Decide by ear whether that reads as patient or as broken.
Weights are under OpenRAIL-M (read the use restrictions), and the upstream GitHub repository appears to have been archived in July 2026.
fix: Spell out every digit before synthesis, speak OTPs and phone numbers one digit per comma, and read critical numbers back for confirmation.
Keep 5 or more steps for Hindi; do not copy English speed settings.
Cap inter-sentence silence at about 700 ms when using slow speeds.
Run a native-listener test before using it for Marathi; if it passes, it replaces two Piper voices with one model.

mms.verdict: Covers Marathi on paper, fails in practice. Prototype fallback only.
good: One recipe for 1,100+ languages, Marathi included; 114 MB per language, about 240 MB RAM, 3.8x real time.
bad: Its alphabet has no digits and no Latin letters, and it skips them silently: the OTP sentence was spoken without the OTP, and the Hinglish sentence lost every English word. In a form assistant that is a wrong answer delivered confidently.
It ignores commas: one pause where other engines make four to six, so instructions arrive as a wall of speech.
Barely responds to the speed control: a 1.4x request gave 1.13–1.18x.
16 kHz output with 8 kHz of bandwidth sounds like a phone line.
Highest ASR error in every language: English 9.8%, Hindi 12.6%, Marathi 27.1%. 'Aadhaar card' was heard as 'here at ecker'.
One voice per language, so no multi-speaker scenes; CC-BY-NC licence rules out a paid product.
fix: A full normaliser is mandatory: every number in words and every English word in Devanagari (scenario 6 shows all the words returning).
Insert the comma pauses yourself by synthesising phrase by phrase.
Realistically, replace it with a fine-tuned Piper Marathi voice.

kitten.verdict: Remarkably clear for 15 million parameters, but English only, so not a candidate for Kaabil.
good: English ASR error 1.0%, level with Piper, from a 57 MB model (25 MB as int8) using under 200 MB RAM.
8.8x real time; 8 voices.
bad: English only.
Speaks about 30% slower than the others at the same speed setting (9.7 against 13–16 characters per second) because of the vendor's built-in speed prior.
Dull top end: 7.5 kHz of bandwidth in a 24 kHz file.
Packaging is awkward: the PyPI package of the same name is not the official one, and the official wheel pulls in PyTorch and spaCy. The rig uses a 40-line ONNX adapter instead.
fix: Set speed to about 1.25 to match the others.
Worth revisiting only if KittenML ships Hindi.

edge.verdict: The bar to beat on number handling and pausing. A cloud service reached through an unofficial door: reference only.
good: The only engine that read raw numbers correctly in all three languages: ₹25,000 as पच्चीस हज़ार रुपए, 03/12/2026 as 3 दिसंबर (day first), 5:30 as साढ़े पाँच.
Pauses like a person: 3.2 s of pauses in the Hindi form prompt at normal speed, against 0.6 s for Piper and 1.3 s for Kokoro. Exact speed control.
Widest pitch movement (±3.7–4.5 semitones) and real Indian-English, Hindi and Marathi voices.
bad: Needs a connection. Single requests took 2–5 s here and one seven-turn conversation took 60 s. On rural networks that is the failure you will see.
Text leaves the device, and this endpoint is unofficial with no guarantee it keeps working.
Only two voices per Indian language.
fix: For production use an official service hosted in India: Azure Speech (the same voices), Sarvam Bulbul or BHASHINI.
Use it now to pre-render Kaabil's fixed prompts for listening tests, so you know what 'good' sounds like before choosing an offline voice.

sections.title: What the hard scenarios showed
sections.lede: Each bullet names something to listen for on the Listen tab.
points: Person in a hurry (1.4x). English stayed fully intelligible on every engine. In Hindi all but MMS stayed under 8% error. Supertonic, Kokoro and the cloud voice actually reach the requested speed; Piper reaches 1.29x and MMS barely moves. None of the small models changes its tone when rushed; they only speak faster. Real urgency (clipped words, rising pitch) needs a model with style control: ElevenLabs audio tags, Gemini style prompts, or Indic Parler-TTS descriptions.

Three people talking at once. No model here generates overlapping speech itself. The rig synthesises each speaker with a different voice, pans them left, right and centre, and overlaps the turns by up to 1.3 s. Supertonic and the cloud voice stayed separable (about 1% error in Hindi); Piper and Kokoro lost 13–14%; MMS has one voice, so its 'three people' are one person interrupting themselves. Native multi-speaker generation exists only in large or commercial models (Gemini TTS, ElevenLabs dialogue mode, VibeVoice, Dia), none of which run on a phone or cover Marathi.
Numbers. The single biggest practical finding. Raw digits broke every local model in at least one language; pre-normalised text fixed nearly all of it. Compare scenarios 3 and 4.

Mixed Hindi-English. Supertonic and the cloud voice read Latin-script English correctly. Kokoro manages after the patch. Piper mangles it and MMS drops it. Writing the English words in Devanagari first (scenario 6) rescues both.
Consent question. Whether the listener hears a question depends on rising pitch at the end, which the transcript cannot show. Listen to this one yourself; it matters for informed consent.

Slow repeat for an elderly listener. What separates the engines is pausing, not speed. The cloud voice leaves three to five times more silence between phrases than Piper or Kokoro at any speed; Supertonic slows mainly by lengthening pauses; Kokoro and Piper stretch the sounds. Build slow mode from normal-speed phrases with inserted silence.

sections.title: What your app must do, whichever voice you choose
sections.lede: These fixes are worth more than swapping one small model for another.
points: Text normalisation in Hindi, Marathi and English: numbers, ₹ amounts, dates (day first), times, phone numbers and OTPs digit by digit, abbreviations (OTP, ITI, UPI).
Transliterate Latin-script words to Devanagari before any model except Supertonic.
Sentence-level streaming: play the first sentence while the next is being synthesised. This hides most of the latency of the slower models.
Read-back for anything that costs money or identity: speak the OTP or amount, then ask the user to confirm.
A replay button and a slower replay, built from pauses, for elderly users.
Cache: every sentence you synthesise more than once should be stored as audio.

sections.title: Not tested here, and why
points: Large open models (Fish Audio Drama 3, Chatterbox, VibeVoice, Dia, IndicF5): they need a GPU with 8 GB or more of memory. This laptop has integrated graphics only.
AI4Bharat Indic Parler-TTS: the strongest open Hindi/Marathi model with emotion control, but the download is gated behind your own Hugging Face account. The adapter is in place; see README.
Commercial APIs (ElevenLabs, Sarvam, Cartesia and others): they need your API keys, which I cannot create or enter. ElevenLabs and Sarvam adapters are in place but have never been run.
Real phones: all speed figures are from a laptop CPU. Measure on your actual 2 GB target before committing.

landscape.title: The premier commercial voices (November 2026)
landscape.lede: Ranked by blind human preference on the Artificial Analysis speech arena, which is English-only, plus the Indian-language specialists. None of these was run in this rig. Hindi and Marathi support is from vendor documentation as I recall it or as found in search; confirm on the vendor's current language list before relying on it.

items.name: Eleven v4 / v4 Turbo
items.what: Current preference leader. Emotion and delivery steered by inline audio tags; dialogue mode with several speakers.
items.indic: Hindi yes. Marathi was listed for v3; confirm for v4.
items.note: The realism ceiling. Useful for pre-rendering fixed prompts; too costly and network-bound for every reply.

items.name: Sarvam Bulbul v3 / v4 Flash
items.what: Indian-language specialist. v3 covers 11 languages; v4 Flash has 200+ persona voices including an English-Hindi code-mixed style. Pace control, built-in text normalisation.
items.note: The most natural fit for Kaabil's online path: Indian accents, code-mixing and data residency. A vendor-run benchmark puts its Hindi above ElevenLabs; treat that as a claim to verify.

items.name: Cartesia Sonic 3.6
items.what: Very low latency streaming voice built for phone agents.
items.indic: Sonic 3 added Hindi and other Indian languages; confirm Marathi.
items.runs: Cloud API. About $49 per million characters.
items.note: Candidate for the IVR / callback channel where response time matters most.

items.name: Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS
items.what: Style controlled by a natural-language prompt; native two-speaker generation.
items.indic: Earlier Gemini TTS listed Hindi and Marathi; confirm for this version.
items.runs: Cloud API. About $16 per million characters.
items.note: Cheapest of the leaders and the easiest way to get 'say this urgently' or a two-person scene.

items.name: Lightning V3.1 Pro
items.what: Fast, low-cost voice from an Indian company.
items.runs: Cloud API. About $20 per million characters.

items.name: Qwen-Audio 3.1 TTS Plus, Speechify Simba 3.5, Inworld Realtime TTS-2
items.note: Strong in English arenas; no evidence here that they beat the Indic specialists in Hindi or Marathi.

items.name: BHASHINI / AI4Bharat services
items.what: Public speech services for 22 Indian languages.
items.note: Already in your architecture slide. Lower polish than Sarvam, but free, public and aligned with the deployment story.

landscape.title: Open models that need a GPU
landscape.lede: These are what 'as human as possible, self-hosted' means today. They belong on a server in your India region, not on the phone.

items.name: Indic Parler-TTS
items.what: You describe the voice in words (speaker, pace, emotion) and it follows.
items.indic: Hindi and Marathi, plus 18 more. Emotion prompts officially supported for Marathi.
items.runs: GPU server. Many times slower than real time on CPU.
items.note: The open model most relevant to Kaabil's server side: real Marathi, emotion control, permissive licence.

items.name: IndicF5
items.what: Flow-matching model that clones a voice from a short reference clip.
items.indic: 11 Indian languages including Hindi and Marathi.
items.note: Lets you build one consistent 'Saathi' voice across languages from a single voice actor.

items.name: Fish Audio Drama 3
items.what: Highest-ranked open-weights model in the arena, level with commercial leaders.
items.runs: GPU server; check the licence terms.
items.note: Proof that open weights have caught up in English.

items.name: Chatterbox / Chatterbox Multilingual
items.what: Zero-shot cloning with an emotion-intensity dial; the multilingual build covers 23 languages.
items.indic: Hindi in the multilingual build; no Marathi.
items.note: Easy licence and expressive, but Hindi only.

items.name: VibeVoice, Dia / Dia2
items.what: Generate whole multi-speaker conversations in one pass, with turn-taking.
items.note: The only open models that natively produce several people talking. No Indian languages.

landscape.title: A note on 'Antimatter'
landscape.lede: I could not find a voice model by that name. The closest match is antimattr, a Y Combinator-backed startup building voice-AI wearables (a ring and earbuds). It makes hardware, not a speech model, so it is not in these tables. If you meant a different product, tell me the spelling and I will add it.
